opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think it's one of the most exciting directions right now, and also one of the most misunderstood.

The core intuition is very appealing: not every token deserves the same amount of compute. If you're predicting "the" after "on top of", you don't need the full model firing. But if you're in the middle of a hard reasoning step or a tricky piece of code, you want everything you've got. Mixture-of-experts is one way to get at that. You decouple the total number of parameters from the compute you spend per token, so you get a lot more capacity for roughly the same FLOPs.

Where I'd be a bit careful is that people often equate sparsity with efficiency, and in practice it's not that simple. On paper you're activating a fraction of the parameters. But then you hit the real-world stuff: memory bandwidth, communication between devices when experts are sharded, load balancing so that some experts aren't overloaded while others sit idle, and training instabilities. A lot of the engineering effort goes into making the theoretical savings actually show up on the hardware. So when I read a paper, the first question I ask is: did this hold at scale, on real infrastructure, or is it a nice FLOP count on a small model?

The second thing is the distinction between routing to *different* computation and actually *skipping* computation. Classic MoE still uses a fixed amount of compute per token, it just picks which experts. The more interesting frontier, to me, is adaptive compute: early exiting, layer skipping, models that can decide to think longer or shorter. That's closer to the real idea that compute should scale with difficulty. And I think there's a nice connection with what we've seen in reasoning models, where you spend more tokens at inference time on hard problems. That's adaptive compute at the sequence level instead of inside the network. Long term, I suspect those two ideas converge: models that allocate compute dynamically both inside the architecture and across the generation.

So my overall assessment: very promising, clearly part of how frontier models get scaled efficiently, but the value is in the details. The research that impresses me most is the work that's honest about the systems costs and shows gains that survive at scale, not just elegant routing schemes on toy setups.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think it's one of the most exciting directions, and I say that as someone who spent a lot of time on the dense side with Llama. The intuition is simple: not every token deserves the same amount of compute. When you're predicting "the" after "of", you don't need the full capacity of the model. When you're in the middle of a hard reasoning step, you do. Dense transformers spend exactly the same FLOPs on both, which is kind of absurd when you think about it.

Mixture-of-experts, in its classic form, addresses the capacity side of that. You get a model with many more parameters than you actually activate per token, so you decouple knowledge from inference cost. DeepSeek, Mixtral, and now basically everyone at the frontier has shown that this works and that the scaling laws are favorable. That part is no longer research, it's engineering.

The more interesting question for me is the second part of what you said, skipping computation, which is adaptive depth rather than adaptive width. Mixture-of-depths, early exit, letting the router decide not just which expert but whether to go through a layer at all. That's closer to what you'd want from a system that "thinks more" on hard tokens and less on easy ones. And it connects naturally to what we've seen with inference-time compute: chain-of-thought is, in some sense, a very crude form of adaptive compute where the model decides to spend more tokens. Doing that inside the architecture, per token, per layer, is the elegant version.

Where I'm more skeptical is the gap between papers and production. Routing is notoriously unstable to train. Load balancing losses interfere with the objective you actually care about. The gains on perplexity sometimes don't translate to downstream capabilities, especially for reasoning, where you'd expect adaptive compute to matter most. And a lot of these papers evaluate at small scale, where the dynamics are just different. My rule from the Llama days is that I don't believe an architectural trick until I see it hold at the scale where it matters, with the same data and the same training budget as the dense baseline.

The other thing people underestimate is the systems cost. Skipping computation sounds free, but if your batching, your KV cache, and your hardware are built around uniform compute per token, irregular compute can be slower in practice than the theoretical FLOP count suggests. So you need the algorithm and the systems co-designed.

So my assessment is: the direction is clearly right, the current instantiations are partially there, and the real test is whether adaptive compute helps on the things that are hard, not just on average loss. If someone shows me a model that reliably spends ten times more compute on the token where the proof breaks than on the filler words around it, and that this improves reasoning at scale, that's a big deal. We're not quite there, but I think we will be.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a promising direction, because you don’t necessarily need the same amount of computation for every input. If something is easy, ideally you spend less compute; if it’s difficult, you spend more. Mixture-of-experts is one way to move toward that, by activating only part of the model.

But I would distinguish activating fewer parameters from learning how much computation a problem actually needs. They’re related, but they’re not exactly the same thing. The question for me is whether the model learns to allocate computation effectively—and whether that translates into better quality for the same real inference cost. Skipping computation is useful if you can preserve the capabilities you care about.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a very promising direction. You don’t necessarily need to activate every parameter for every token. With mixture of experts, you can have a lot of capacity while using only part of it for a given input.

But I would separate that from learning how much computation a problem needs. Selecting a few experts isn’t quite the same as deciding, “This is easy, I can stop here,” or, “This is difficult, I should spend more compute.” That second question is especially interesting.

And ultimately, you have to measure the actual efficiency. If you save computation but introduce communication overhead or make the hardware harder to utilize, the practical gain can be smaller than it looks. So I’m excited about it, but I’d judge it by quality at a given latency and cost, rather than just the number of active parameters.
